a: When Jesus finished these words
t: The end of the fourth discourse
p: Matthew closes each of Jesus' five long speeches with this same formula.
b: Matthew ends each of the five great speeches of Jesus with almost the same words: 7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1. Here it closes the speech about life in the church (chapter 18). Many readers see in the five speeches an echo of the five books of Moses, with Jesus as the teacher of a new Torah, though scholars debate how far Matthew meant the pattern. The formula itself echoes the way Deuteronomy marks the end of Moses' speeches (Deuteronomy 31:24; 32:45).

a: the territory of Judea on the far side of the Jordan
p: Jesus takes the eastern road south, through Perea, the region ruled by Herod Antipas.
b: Strictly, the land east of the Jordan was Perea, not Judea. Galilean pilgrims going to Jerusalem often went down the east side of the river to avoid Samaria, then crossed near Jericho (20:29). Matthew's wording may mean "the parts of Judea, and the land beyond the Jordan," or may simply name the whole journey's area. Mark 10:1 has the same phrase with "and." From here on, everything in Matthew happens on the road to Jerusalem or in the city.

a: to test him
t: Why the question was a trap
p: Divorce was a live and dangerous issue: John the Baptist had been killed over Herod's marriage.
b: The Pharisees were not asking an idle question. Jesus was now in the territory of Herod Antipas, who had divorced his first wife to marry Herodias, and John the Baptist had been killed for condemning it (14:3–12). A strict answer could put Jesus in the same danger. Among Jewish teachers the question was also a real dispute between two schools (see the next note), so any answer would offend someone.

a: on any ground at all
t: "For any cause": a phrase from a debate
p: The Greek echoes a Jewish legal slogan: the school of Hillel allowed divorce "for any matter."
b: The Mishnah records a dispute on Deuteronomy 24:1, where a man divorces his wife because he found "something indecent" (Hebrew 'ervat davar) in her. The school of Shammai read it narrowly: only for sexual misconduct. The school of Hillel read the two words separately, as "indecency" or "a matter," so a man could divorce her even if she spoiled his food; Rabbi Akiva added, even if he found someone prettier (Mishnah Gittin 9:10). Josephus, who says he followed the Pharisees' way of life (Life 12), says a man may divorce his wife "for any cause whatsoever" (Antiquities 4.253). David Instone-Brewer argues that "for any cause" was the Hillelite technical term, so the question means: do you side with Hillel? Mark's version lacks the phrase (Mark 10:2).
orig: κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν (kata pasan aitian), 'according to every cause'

a: made them 'male and female' at the start
p: Jesus answers a question about Deuteronomy by going behind it to Genesis 1 and 2.
b: Jesus quotes Genesis 1:27 ("male and female he created them") and then Genesis 2:24 (19:5). His argument is that the order of creation shows God's purpose, and a later law that allows divorce cannot overturn that purpose. A similar move appears in the Damascus Document, a rule book of a Jewish group related to Qumran, which uses "male and female he created them" against taking a second wife while the first is alive (CD 4:20–5:2). So Jesus' strict view had company among Jews of his time.

a: the two will become one flesh
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 2:24 says "they become one flesh"; the Greek Bible adds "the two."
b: This site's Plain of Genesis 2:24 reads: "So a man leaves his father and his mother and sticks close to his wife, and they become one flesh." Jesus' quotation follows the Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, which reads "the two shall be one flesh" (so also the Samaritan Pentateuch). The word "two" sharpens the point: marriage is between two, not more. Jesus then draws the conclusion himself: "no longer two, but one flesh" (19:6). Paul quotes the same verse in the same form (1 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 5:31).
orig: οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν (hoi dyo eis sarka mian)

a: yoked together
p: The verb pictures two animals under one yoke: a working partnership God himself puts in place.
b: The Greek verb syzeugnymi means to put under one yoke. It was a common word for marriage in Greek, and the noun syzygos, "yokefellow," could mean a spouse. Jesus makes God the one who yokes. "No human being should separate" is aimed first at the husband, who in Jewish and Roman law could end the marriage himself, and then at any court that approves.

a: Why then did Moses order
p: The Pharisees say Moses "ordered" it; Jesus answers that Moses only "let" it happen.
b: Deuteronomy 24:1–4 does not command divorce. It assumes divorce happens and regulates it: the husband must give a written document (Hebrew sefer keritut), and he may not later remarry her after she has married another. The document protected the woman, because it proved she was free to remarry. Jesus corrects the Pharisees' verb: Moses "let you" (19:8). In Mark the roles are reversed: Jesus asks what Moses commanded, and the Pharisees answer that Moses permitted (Mark 10:3–4).

a: hard-heartedness
p: The law met people where they were. The word is the Greek Bible's term for a heart that will not listen.
b: Sklērokardia appears in the Greek of Deuteronomy 10:16 and Jeremiah 4:4, where Israel is told to "circumcise" the heart. Jesus treats the divorce law as a concession to human stubbornness, not as God's ideal. Christians and Jews have long used this idea, that some laws limit damage rather than describe the best, for other parts of the Torah too, such as slavery and war captives.

a: except for sexual sin
p: Only Matthew has this exception. What porneia means here, and what it allows, divides churches.
b: Mark 10:11–12 and Luke 16:18 have no exception; Matthew has it here and at 5:32. The Greek porneia is a broad word for sexual sin (see the topic page). Readings: (1) adultery by the wife, which allows divorce and, for most Protestants, remarriage (Erasmus, Luther, Westminster); (2) adultery allows separation but not remarriage (Augustine, Jerome, Catholic teaching); (3) a marriage within forbidden degrees of kinship (Leviticus 18; compare Acts 15:20, 29), so it was never a true marriage; (4) unfaithfulness during betrothal, as Joseph suspected of Mary (1:18–19). Many scholars see Matthew siding with the school of Shammai, which allowed divorce only for sexual misconduct. See the "Where Christians differ" card on the chapter page.
orig: μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ (mē epi porneia), 'not for porneia'

a: it is not worth getting married
p: Their reaction shows how strict Jesus' teaching sounded in a world where men could end a marriage easily.
b: If a man cannot get out of a marriage, say the disciples, better not to get in. The word translated "position" (aitia) is the "ground" of 19:3: if divorce "for any ground" is gone, what ground is left? Their dismay assumes the common practice of easy divorce for men. Jesus does not soften his answer. Instead he speaks about those who do not marry at all (19:11–12). Some readers take "this saying" in 19:11 to mean the disciples' remark (not marrying is a gift only some have); others take it to mean Jesus' teaching on divorce (only those given grace can keep it).

a: There are eunuchs who were born that way
p: Eunuchs served kings and temples, but the Law kept a castrated man out of the assembly.
b: A eunuch was a castrated man, often a slave serving in a palace or a temple (Esther 2:3; Acts 8:27). Deuteronomy 23:1 excluded such a man from the LORD's assembly, but Isaiah 56:3–5 promised faithful eunuchs "a name better than sons and daughters." Jesus names three kinds: those born unable to have children, those made eunuchs by others, and those who "made themselves eunuchs" for the kingdom, which nearly all readers take as a picture of choosing not to marry. Jesus himself was unmarried, as were John the Baptist and later Paul (1 Corinthians 7:7–8).
r: Deuteronomy 23:1; Isaiah 56:3–5; Wisdom of Solomon 3:14; Acts 8:27–39; 1 Corinthians 7:7–8, 32–35

a: who made themselves eunuchs because of the kingdom of heaven
p: Origen of Alexandria is said to have taken this literally. The church soon forbade it.
b: Eusebius reports that the young Origen castrated himself, taking this verse too literally (Church History 6.8); later, in his commentary on Matthew, Origen himself warned against a literal reading. The Council of Nicaea (AD 325, canon 1) barred self-castrated men from the clergy. Nearly every interpreter, Jewish and Christian, ancient and modern, reads the saying as figurative: people who give up marriage to serve God's kingdom. A minority of modern scholars think it first answered a taunt: Jesus' enemies may have called the unmarried Jesus and his followers "eunuchs."

a: lay his hands on them and pray
p: Parents asked a holy man to bless their children, as Jacob blessed his grandsons.
b: Laying hands on someone with a prayer was a way to give a blessing, as Jacob blessed Ephraim and Manasseh (Genesis 48:14–16). The disciples treat the children as an interruption. In that world children had little status, which is the point of Jesus' answer.

a: The kingdom of heaven is for people like them
p: Jesus does not say children are innocent. He says the kingdom belongs to the small and dependent.
b: The Greek is literally "of such ones is the kingdom." Jesus has already said that to enter the kingdom one must turn and become like children (18:3–4). Children here stand for those who have nothing to bring and must receive. The verse was used from early times in arguments about baptizing infants: Tertullian cited it while urging delay (On Baptism 18), and Luther's baptismal service reads its parallel in Mark. See the "Where Christians differ" card on the chapter page.

a: what is the good I should do
p: In Matthew the man asks what good thing to do; in Mark and Luke he calls Jesus "good teacher."
b: Matthew's wording differs from Mark 10:17 and Luke 18:18 in a way that matters. There the man says "Good teacher," and Jesus answers, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone." In Matthew the adjective moves to the question: "what good thing," and Jesus answers "Why are you asking me about the good?" Many scholars think Matthew changed Mark to avoid any hint that Jesus denied his own goodness. Later copyists of Matthew made it match Mark again (see the variants on 19:16–17).

a: Only One is good
t: Is Jesus saying he is not good?
p: Jesus points the man to God, the one source of goodness, and then to God's commands.
b: Some readers hear Jesus quietly claiming to be God ("if only God is good, and you call me good..."); others hear him deflecting praise to the Father, as a faithful Jew would. In Matthew's form the question is about "the good," a common topic for Jewish teachers, who said that the good is the Torah (Mishnah Avot 6:3). Jesus' answer fits that: the One who is good has already said what is good. "Enter into life" means to enter eternal life, the life of the age to come (19:16, 29).

a: You must not murder
p: Jesus quotes the second table of the Ten Commandments, the ones about neighbors, and adds Leviticus 19:18.
b: Jesus names the commands about other people: murder, adultery, theft, false witness, honoring parents (Exodus 20:12–16; Deuteronomy 5:16–20), and then the summary, "You are to love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18), which only Matthew adds here. He does not list the command against coveting, which Mark replaces with "do not defraud" (Mark 10:19). The man's test will come at exactly the point of coveting: his possessions (19:21–22). The wording here follows this site's Plain of Exodus 20 where the Greek allows.

a: The young man
p: Only Matthew calls him young; only Luke calls him a ruler. Together they give the familiar "rich young ruler."
b: Matthew alone calls him a young man (neaniskos, a man in his twenties or thirties), Luke alone calls him "a ruler" (Luke 18:18), and all three say he was rich. The popular name "rich young ruler" combines the Gospels. In Mark, "Jesus fixed his eyes on him and loved him" (Mark 10:21), a detail Matthew leaves out.

a: If you wish to be perfect
p: The Greek teleios means whole, mature, complete. It recalls 5:48: "perfect, the way your heavenly Father is perfect."
b: Only Matthew uses teleios in the Gospels, here and at 5:48. It means complete or whole, not sinless: the Hebrew behind it would be tamim, "wholehearted" (Genesis 17:1; Deuteronomy 18:13). The young man has kept the commands but lacks one thing, an undivided heart. From the 300s on, this verse was read as a "counsel of perfection": a higher calling of poverty for some Christians beyond the commandments for all, and it led Antony of Egypt to give away his property and go into the desert (Athanasius, Life of Antony 2). Protestant reformers rejected the two-level reading. See the "Where Christians differ" card on the chapter page.

a: You will have treasure in heaven
p: Giving to the poor stores up treasure with God, a Jewish idea Jesus has already taught.
b: Jesus has said, "pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven" (6:20). Jewish teaching said the same of almsgiving: "Store up your treasure as the Most High commands" (Sirach 29:11), and "alms rescue from death" (Tobit 4:10; 12:9). The command to sell everything was for this man, not a rule Jesus gave to all who followed him: Zacchaeus gives half (Luke 19:8), and women of means supported Jesus from their property (Luke 8:3).

a: a camel could get through a needle's eye
p: An image of the impossible. The "Needle Gate" in Jerusalem and the "rope" readings are later inventions.
b: Jesus uses a deliberately absurd picture: the largest animal in the land through the smallest hole. The Babylonian Talmud has a similar saying with an elephant (Berakhot 55b; Bava Metzia 38b). Two popular explanations soften it. One says there was a small gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye, which a camel could pass on its knees; there is no ancient evidence for such a gate. The other says kamēlos (camel) should be kamilos (rope); a few late manuscripts read that, but it is a scribal "improvement." The disciples' reaction (19:25) shows they took it as impossible, and Jesus agrees: only God can do it (19:26).

a: the kingdom of God
p: Matthew almost always says "kingdom of heaven"; here he keeps "kingdom of God" in the very next verse.
b: Matthew uses "kingdom of heaven" about thirty times and "kingdom of God" only four or five times (12:28; 19:24; 21:31, 43; and in some manuscripts 6:33). The two mean the same: "heaven" was a respectful Jewish way to say "God." Why he switches here is unclear. Some think he kept Mark's wording; others that he chose "God" for emphasis in sayings of judgment.

a: Who can be saved, then?
p: Wealth was often seen as a sign of God's blessing. If the rich cannot enter, who can?
b: Deuteronomy promised prosperity to the obedient (Deuteronomy 28:1–14), and many assumed the rich were blessed by God. Others in Israel's tradition warned against trusting in riches (Psalm 49; Proverbs 11:28). Jesus' saying overturns the easy assumption: wealth makes entering harder, not easier. "Saved" here means entering the kingdom and eternal life.

a: when the world is born again
t: The new birth of the world
p: The rare Greek word palingenesia means rebirth. Here it means the renewal of all things at the end.
b: Palingenesia, "genesis again," was used by Stoic philosophers for the rebirth of the world after a cosmic fire, by Josephus for the rebirth of the Jewish nation after the exile (Antiquities 11.66), and in Titus 3:5 for a person's new birth at baptism. Here it is the world to come: Jewish hope looked for a new heaven and new earth (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22), and Revelation pictures it (Revelation 21:1–5). Luke's parallel speaks of "my kingdom" instead (Luke 22:29–30).
r: Isaiah 65:17; Isaiah 66:22; Acts 3:21; Titus 3:5; Revelation 21:1–5; Luke 22:28–30

a: judge the twelve tribes of Israel
p: The Twelve stand for a restored Israel. "Judge" may mean condemn, or rule as the judges of old did.
b: Jesus chose twelve disciples as a sign that God was gathering all twelve tribes again, though ten had been scattered since Assyria. Many Jews hoped for that regathering (Ezekiel 37:15–28; Psalms of Solomon 17:26–28). "Judge" can mean to pass sentence on Israel, or to rule and defend Israel, as the "judges" of the book of Judges did. E. P. Sanders took this saying as strong evidence that the historical Jesus expected Israel's restoration. Revelation 21:12–14 sets the names of the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles on the new Jerusalem.
r: Luke 22:30; Ezekiel 37:15–28; Daniel 7:9–10, 22; Psalms of Solomon 17:26–28; Revelation 21:12–14

a: a hundred times as much
p: Mark adds "now in this age... with persecutions"; Matthew points only to the age to come.
b: Mark 10:30 says the reward comes "now, in this present time: homes, brothers, sisters... along with persecutions. And in the age that is coming he will get eternal life." Matthew drops the "now" and the list of present gains. Many readers find the present reward in the new family of the church (12:48–50). The promise has been misused by preachers of a "prosperity gospel" who teach that giving money brings a hundredfold financial return; most churches reject that reading.

a: many of the first will be last, and the last will be first
p: This saying, turned around in 20:16, wraps the parable of the workers in the vineyard.
b: Matthew sets the same saying before and after the parable of the workers (20:1–16), in reverse order: first/last here, last/first in 20:16. The parable shows what it means. The word "many" leaves room: not every first is last. The saying appears in other settings too (Mark 10:31; Luke 13:30), so Jesus likely used it more than once.

a: workers for his vineyard
p: Hired by the day, paid at evening: the poorest free workers in Galilee and Judea.
b: Day laborers owned no land and had no steady job. They waited in the market square to be hired. The Law required that they be paid before sunset (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15), because a family might eat that night only if the day's wage came in. Grape harvest was the busiest time, when owners needed extra hands quickly before rain or heat spoiled the crop.

a: one denarius for the day's work
p: A Roman silver coin, the usual pay for a day of farm work.
b: The denarius was a silver coin stamped with the emperor's head (22:19–21). It was the standard daily wage for a laborer and enough to feed a family for a day. Tobit 5:15 has a drachma, a similar Greek coin, as a daily wage. The amount was fair but not generous: a family living on it lived from day to day.

a: the third hour
p: Hours were counted from sunrise, about 6 a.m. The third hour is about 9 a.m.
b: Jews and Romans divided daylight into twelve hours, so the length of an hour changed with the season. The third hour was mid-morning (about 9 a.m.), the sixth noon, the ninth mid-afternoon (about 3 p.m.), and the eleventh about 5 p.m., with one hour of work left before sunset. The English phrase "at the eleventh hour" comes from this parable.

a: is your eye evil because I am good?
p: "An evil eye" is a Hebrew idiom for envy or stinginess, not a magic curse.
b: In Hebrew and Aramaic, a "bad eye" ('ayin ra'ah) means a grudging, envious attitude, and a "good eye" means generosity (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 22:9; 28:22; Mishnah Avot 2:9). Jesus used the idiom in 6:22–23. The owner's question sets his "good" against the worker's "evil eye": the complaint is not about injustice, since the worker got what he agreed to, but about resentment at someone else's good fortune.
orig: ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου πονηρός (ho ophthalmos sou ponēros)

a: the last first, and the first last
p: Grace, Israel and the Gentiles, early and late converts, or justice for the poor? Readings differ.
b: The parable has been read in several ways. (1) Grace: God's reward is a gift, not wages earned by hours (Augustine; Luther). (2) Salvation history: the early workers are Israel or the Jewish leaders, the late ones are tax collectors, sinners and Gentiles (Irenaeus; Jeremias). (3) Life stages: people called early or late in life, even on the deathbed, receive the same eternal life (Chrysostom; Gregory the Great). (4) Social reading: a landowner who pays every worker enough to live shows what God's justice looks like (Herzog, Schottroff). In Matthew's context it answers Peter's question, "What will there be for us?" (19:27).

a: the chief priests and scribes
p: Each of Jesus' three predictions of his death adds detail. This one names Gentiles and crucifixion.
b: Jesus has predicted his death at 16:21 and 17:22–23. Here, for the first time in Matthew, he names who will do what: Jewish leaders will condemn him, Gentiles (the Romans) will mock, whip and crucify him. Only Matthew says "crucify" in this prediction (Mark 10:34 says "kill"). The "third day" echoes Hosea 6:2.

a: the mother of Zebedee's sons
p: In Mark, James and John ask for themselves. In Matthew their mother asks.
b: In Mark 10:35 the brothers make the request themselves. Matthew has their mother speak, but Jesus answers the sons ("You have no idea what you are asking for" is plural), and the other ten are angry with the brothers, not her. Some think Matthew wanted to spare the apostles; others that he records a real detail. She may be the woman named among the watchers at the cross (27:56). A late tradition, based on comparing 27:56 with Mark 15:40 and John 19:25, names her Salome and makes her Mary's sister, which would make James and John Jesus' cousins; this is uncertain.

a: one on your right and one on your left
p: The seats beside a king were for his closest officials. At the cross, two criminals take them.
b: To sit at a king's right and left was to share his rule (1 Kings 2:19; Psalm 110:1). The mother asks for this in the coming kingdom, after Jesus has just promised the Twelve thrones (19:28). The irony is sharp: when Jesus is enthroned as "King of the Jews" on the cross, the places at his right and left are taken by two bandits (27:38).

a: the cup
p: In the prophets, the cup is God's judgment to be drunk. Jesus will pray about this cup in Gethsemane.
b: In the Hebrew Bible the "cup" often stands for God's wrath poured out (Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15–28; Psalm 75:8), though it can also mean one's lot in life, good or bad (Psalm 16:5; 23:5). Jesus' cup is his suffering and death (26:39, 42). He says the brothers will drink it too: James was killed by Herod Agrippa about AD 44 (Acts 12:2). Tradition says John lived to old age, so many take his "cup" as suffering and exile (Revelation 1:9).

a: he will be your servant
p: Two words: diakonos (servant, one who waits on others) and doulos (slave, the lowest status).
b: Jesus climbs down the social ladder: whoever wants to be great will be a diakonos, a servant who waits at table, and whoever wants to be first will be a doulos, a slave owned by another. In the Roman world, where honor and rank governed everything, this reversed the normal order. The church's word "deacon" comes from diakonos. "Will be" can be read as a command ("must be") or as a description of how things work in the kingdom.

a: a ransom in place of many
p: Lytron was the price paid to free a slave or captive. "Many" echoes Isaiah's suffering servant.
b: Lytron is the price paid to set someone free: a slave, a prisoner of war, a life forfeited by law (Exodus 21:30; Numbers 35:31). Anti means "in place of." "Many" in Hebrew idiom can mean "all," the great number, as in Isaiah 53:11–12, where the servant "bore the sin of many." Christians have read the verse in several ways: the church fathers often asked to whom the ransom was paid (Origen said the devil; Gregory of Nazianzus rejected that); Anselm and the Reformers read it as satisfaction or penalty paid to God's justice; others stress the picture of liberation without pressing who receives the price.
r: Mark 10:45; Isaiah 53:10–12; 26:28; 1 Timothy 2:5–6; Titus 2:14; 1 Peter 1:18–19; Exodus 21:30

a: two blind men
p: Mark and Luke tell of one blind man; Matthew has two, as he does with the demoniacs at Gadara.
b: Mark names one man, Bartimaeus, as Jesus leaves Jericho (Mark 10:46–52); Luke has one man as Jesus approaches Jericho (Luke 18:35–43). Matthew has two men and no name, and he has a similar pair of blind men in 9:27–31 and two demoniacs in 8:28 (Mark has one). Explanations: Matthew knew of a second man; Matthew doubles witnesses because the Law required two (Deuteronomy 19:15); or Matthew combined this healing with another. Harmonizers note that there were two Jerichos, the old town and Herod's new one, which could explain "leaving" and "approaching."

a: Lord, show us mercy, Son of David!
p: Blind men see what Jerusalem's leaders will not: Jesus is the royal heir. The cry became the church's Kyrie.
b: "Son of David" is a royal title for the Messiah (1:1; 22:42). In Matthew it is used most often by people in need: blind men, a Canaanite woman, and children (9:27; 15:22; 21:15). Solomon, David's son, was known in Jewish legend as a healer and exorcist (Josephus, Antiquities 8.45–49), which may explain why healing and the title go together. The Greek Kyrie, eleēson, "Lord, have mercy," became one of the oldest prayers in Christian worship and the Jesus Prayer of the Orthodox tradition.

a: Bethphage, by the Mount of Olives
t: Bethphage and the Mount of Olives
p: A village on the ridge east of Jerusalem, where the road from Jericho comes over the top.
b: Bethphage ("house of unripe figs") lay on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, near Bethany (21:17). The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley. Zechariah 14:4 says the LORD's feet will stand on it on the day he comes to save Jerusalem, so a royal arrival from this direction had special meaning. Later rabbinic texts treat Bethphage as the outer limit of the city for some religious rules.

a: a donkey tied up, and a colt with her
p: Only Matthew has two animals. Did he misread Hebrew poetry, or record a mother and her foal?
b: Mark, Luke and John have only one animal. Zechariah 9:9 says the king rides "on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey," which in Hebrew poetry is one animal described twice. Some critics think Matthew read the poem as speaking of two animals and told the story to match. Others reply that Matthew, a careful Jewish writer, surely knew Hebrew parallelism; an unbroken colt might well be led with its mother to keep it calm, and Matthew mentions both because both were there. Others see a deliberate symbol: an animal never ridden, fit for a sacred use (Numbers 19:2; 1 Samuel 6:7).

a: The Lord has need of them
p: The Greek kyrios can mean God, Jesus, or simply "the master" or "the owner."
b: Ho kyrios could be heard as "the master needs them," a request from an important person. In Matthew's story the reader knows it means Jesus. Some suggest the animals' owner was a follower who had arranged this. "He will send them straight away" probably means the owner will release them; in Mark the words can also be read as Jesus' promise to send them back (Mark 11:3).

a: Tell the daughter of Zion
p: The quotation joins Isaiah 62:11 to Zechariah 9:9 and leaves out "righteous and victorious."
b: "Tell the daughter of Zion" comes from Isaiah 62:11, where it introduces "Look, your salvation is coming!" The rest is Zechariah 9:9, close to the Greek Bible. Matthew leaves out Zechariah's "righteous and having salvation" and keeps "gentle" (Greek praus; Hebrew 'ani, "humble, poor"), the same word Jesus uses of himself in 11:29. Zechariah 9:10 goes on to say the king will end war and "speak peace to the nations." Jewish tradition also read Zechariah 9:9 of the Messiah: the Talmud says that if Israel is worthy, he comes on the clouds (Daniel 7:13); if not, "lowly and riding on a donkey" (Sanhedrin 98a).

a: Jesus sat on top of them
p: The Greek says he sat "on them," meaning most likely on the cloaks.
b: The second "them" (epanō autōn) most naturally means the cloaks just mentioned, though it could mean the animals. Readers who find a picture of Jesus riding two animals at once have taken Matthew too literally, but the grammar is not certain. Spreading cloaks for a new king is an old sign of homage: officers did it for Jehu (2 Kings 9:13).

a: cutting branches off the trees
p: Branches and palms marked festivals and victories, like the Feast of Booths and Hanukkah.
b: Leafy branches were carried at the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:40), when Psalm 118 was sung and worshipers waved the lulav, a bundle of palm, myrtle and willow. Palm branches also greeted Simon Maccabee when he took the Citadel (1 Maccabees 13:51) and were carried at the first Hanukkah (2 Maccabees 10:7). Only John says the branches were palms (John 12:13), which gave the church "Palm Sunday." The scene has the feel of a festival and of a victory parade.
r: Leviticus 23:40; 1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7; John 12:13; Revelation 7:9; Mark 11:8

a: Hosanna to the Son of David!
p: A Hebrew cry meaning "Save, please!" from Psalm 118:25. By Jesus' day it was also a shout of praise.
b: Hosanna is the Greek spelling of Hebrew hoshi'a na, "save, please," the cry of Psalm 118:25 ("LORD, please, save us now!"). Psalm 118 belonged to the Hallel, the psalms sung at the great festivals, and its words had become a welcome for pilgrims and a shout of praise, much like "Hurray!" or "God save the king." "Hosanna to the Son of David" therefore means both "Save us, Son of David" and "Praise to the Son of David." "Hosanna in the highest" calls on heaven itself to join the praise.

a: Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name!
p: The pilgrims' psalm becomes a welcome for the coming king. Jesus will quote it again in 23:39.
b: This site's Plain of Psalm 118:26 reads: "Blessed is the one who comes in the LORD's name! / We bless you, all of you, from the LORD's house." In the psalm, priests greeted pilgrims entering the temple. The crowd applies it to Jesus as "the one who comes," a phrase John the Baptist used of the Messiah (3:11; 11:3). Jesus will quote the same line at the end of his public teaching (23:39). It is sung in the Sanctus of the Christian Eucharist.

a: the entire city was shaken
p: The verb is the root of the word for earthquake. It appears again when Jesus dies and rises.
b: Seiō, "shake," is the verb behind seismos, "earthquake." Matthew uses it at the death of Jesus ("the earth shook," 27:51) and at the resurrection (28:4, where the guards "shook"). The city's question, "Who is this?", recalls the troubled question of 2:3, when the magi announced a newborn king and "all Jerusalem" was disturbed.

a: the prophet, Jesus, the one from Nazareth in Galilee
p: The crowds see Jesus as a prophet, perhaps the prophet like Moses. Matthew's readers know he is more.
b: Many in Jesus' day saw him as a prophet (16:14; 21:46). With the article, "the prophet" may recall the promised prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15–18; John 6:14). Matthew does not reject the title, but his story has already called Jesus Messiah, Son of David and Son of God. Historians widely agree that Jesus was seen by his contemporaries as a prophet; how he saw himself is debated.

a: threw out everyone who was selling and buying in the temple
p: Money changers and dove sellers served pilgrims who needed temple coins and animals for sacrifice.
b: The temple tax had to be paid in silver shekels of Tyre, a coin of reliable purity (Mishnah Shekalim 1:3 says changers set up tables in the temple before Passover). Doves were the offering of the poor (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8). The market was probably in the huge outer court Herod built, the Court of the Gentiles. Why Jesus acted is debated: (1) to protest dishonest trade or greed; (2) to protest the use of the one court where Gentiles could pray; (3) as a prophetic sign that the temple would be destroyed and replaced (E. P. Sanders). Matthew sets it on the day of the entry; Mark the next day (Mark 11:15); John near the start of Jesus' ministry (John 2:13–22).

a: 'My house will be called a house of prayer,'
p: Jesus joins Isaiah's hope for a house of prayer with Jeremiah's warning about a bandits' cave.
b: Isaiah 56:7 promises that foreigners and eunuchs (see 19:12) will be welcome, "for my house will be called a house of prayer for all the peoples." Mark keeps "for all the nations" (Mark 11:17); Matthew and Luke leave it out. Jeremiah 7:11 asks whether the temple has become "a cave of robbers" for people who sin and then hide behind the temple's protection; Jeremiah went on to predict its destruction (Jeremiah 7:14). The Greek lēstēs means a bandit or raider, and later also a rebel: Josephus uses it for the armed rebels who held the temple in AD 66–70.

a: blind and lame people came up to him
t: The blind and the lame in the temple
p: A saying about David kept the blind and lame out of "the house." Jesus heals them inside it.
b: When David took Jerusalem, a saying arose: "No one blind or lame may come into the house" (2 Samuel 5:8). The Qumran texts also kept the blind and lame out of the assembly and the holy city (Temple Scroll 45:12–14; Damascus Document 15:15–17). Only Matthew tells that Jesus, the Son of David, healed them in the temple, turning the old exclusion around.

a: From the mouths of children and babies at the breast you have made praise complete
p: Jesus quotes the Greek Bible, which reads "praise" where the Hebrew has "strength" or "defense."
b: This site's Plain of Psalm 8:2 reads: "Out of the mouths of children and babies at the breast / you have founded a strong defense because of your foes." The Hebrew 'oz means strength; the Septuagint translated it ainos, "praise," and Matthew quotes the Septuagint. The point is the same in both: God uses the weakest voices to silence his enemies. Jesus' "Did you never read" (also 12:3; 19:4; 21:42; 22:31) is a sharp question to experts in the Scriptures.

a: And right then the fig tree dried up
p: A sign acted out: in the prophets a fruitless fig tree pictures Israel under judgment.
b: The prophets used figs for Israel: "I saw your ancestors like the first ripe fig when the tree first bore" (Hosea 9:10), and "no figs on the fig tree" for a people ripe for judgment (Jeremiah 8:13; Micah 7:1). Mark tells this story in two parts, around the temple scene, so that the tree explains the temple (Mark 11:12–25); Mark also says it was not the season for figs. Matthew makes the withering instant and uses it to teach about faith. Most readers take it as a prophetic sign of judgment on a temple leadership with leaves but no fruit (compare 21:43). Some readers find it hard that Jesus cursed a tree; the act is a sign, like the prophets' symbolic acts (Jeremiah 13:1–11; 19:1–13).

a: You could even tell this mountain
p: "Uprooting mountains" was a Jewish figure of speech for doing what seems impossible.
b: Rabbinic texts call a brilliant teacher an "uprooter of mountains" (Talmud, Berakhot 64a). "This mountain," said on the road from Bethany, could be the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4 says it will split) or the temple mount ahead of them, which some read as a hint that the temple will be removed. Paul knows the saying: "faith to move mountains" (1 Corinthians 13:2). It promises the power of trusting prayer, not magic on command.

a: the people's elders
p: The temple's leaders, members of the council that later tried Jesus, challenge his right to act.
b: The chief priests (the high priest's family and senior priests) and the elders (heads of leading families) made up much of the Sanhedrin, the council that governed Jerusalem under Rome (26:3, 57). The temple was their responsibility, so after 21:12–13 they ask for Jesus' credentials. A teacher normally cited his teacher; a prophet claimed a call from God. Jesus answers with a question, as rabbis often did.

a: The baptism of John
p: Jesus ties his authority to John's. The leaders refuse to commit themselves.
b: "From heaven" means "from God" (compare "kingdom of heaven"). If John's call came from God, then John's witness to the one coming after him (3:11–14) supports Jesus. Josephus confirms that John was widely honored as a good man and that many saw Herod's defeat by the Nabateans as God's punishment for killing him (Antiquities 18.116–119). The leaders' answer, "We do not know," is a confession that they will not judge a prophet, so Jesus will not explain himself to them.

a: Afterward he regretted it and went
p: Matthew uses metamelomai here, "regret, think again," not the usual word for repent.
b: The usual word for repentance is metanoeō (3:2; 4:17). Here and in 21:32 Matthew uses metamelomai, "to feel regret, think better of it." Matthew uses it once more, of Judas, who "regretted" what he had done (27:3). The first son's regret turns into action; the leaders, Jesus says, never even regretted (21:32).

a: tax collectors and prostitutes are going ahead of you
p: Two groups Jewish society scorned: one for collaborating with Rome, the other for selling sex.
b: Tax collectors bought the right to collect tolls and taxes and were seen as cheats and collaborators (9:9–11; 11:19). Prostitutes broke the Law's sexual rules, often out of poverty or slavery. Both had responded to John's call (Luke 3:12; 7:29–30). "Going ahead of you" may mean "entering instead of you" or "entering before you," leaving the door open for the leaders to follow. It does not praise their sins; it praises their turning.

a: walking the way of righteousness
p: John lived and taught a right way of life. The phrase recalls Jesus' words to John at his baptism.
b: "The way of righteousness" is a Jewish phrase for a life that pleases God (Proverbs 8:20; 12:28; 16:31). John both taught it and walked it. Matthew links John and righteousness at the start ("to fulfill all righteousness," 3:15). The religious leaders refused John even though they saw sinners changed by him.

a: planted a vineyard
p: Every detail echoes Isaiah 5, where the vineyard is Israel and the owner is the LORD.
b: Isaiah 5:1–7 is a love song about a friend who planted a vineyard, fenced it, built a tower, dug a winepress, and got only sour grapes; it ends: "The vineyard of the LORD of Armies is the house of Israel." Jesus' hearers would hear that song at once. But in Jesus' parable the vineyard bears fruit; the problem is the tenants, who will not give it to the owner. So the judgment falls on those in charge of the vineyard (21:45), not on the vineyard itself. The Gospel of Thomas, an early Christian sayings collection, has a shorter form of the parable (saying 65).
r: Isaiah 5:1–7; Psalm 80:8–16; Jeremiah 2:21; Mark 12:1–12; Luke 20:9–19; Gospel of Thomas 65

a: leased it out to farmers and left the country
p: Large estates owned by distant landlords and worked by tenants were common in Roman Palestine.
b: Papyri from Egypt and other sources show estates leased to tenant farmers who paid a share of the crop. Under Leviticus 19:23–25 the fruit of new vines was forbidden for three years and holy to God in the fourth, so an owner first took a harvest for himself in the fifth year (Jeremias). Disputes, unpaid rents and violence between tenants and agents are well known. Jesus' hearers, many of them poor farmers, would know such tensions. Some modern readers (for example William Herzog) read the parable from the tenants' side, as a story of desperate peasants; Matthew reads it as a story about God and Israel's leaders.

a: he sent them his own son
p: After the slaves (the prophets) comes the son. Matthew's readers hear Jesus' own story.
b: The slaves sent one after another stand for the prophets, many of whom were mistreated or killed (23:29–37; Jeremiah 7:25–26; 2 Chronicles 24:19–21). The son is the owner's last appeal. Matthew changes Mark's order: in Mark the son is killed and then thrown out (Mark 12:8); in Matthew and Luke he is thrown out of the vineyard first, then killed, which many see as matching Jesus' death outside the city (Hebrews 13:12).

a: He will destroy those evil men in an evil way
p: The Greek repeats the word for "evil": bad men, badly destroyed.
b: Kakous kakōs apolesei is a common Greek turn of phrase, "he will destroy the wretches wretchedly." In Matthew the hearers pronounce the verdict on themselves, as David did when Nathan told him the parable of the poor man's lamb (2 Samuel 12:1–7). In Mark and Luke, Jesus answers his own question.

a: A stone that the builders threw out has become the head of the corner
p: Psalm 118:22, from the same psalm the crowds sang at the entry, was a favorite text of the early church.
b: This site's Plain of Psalm 118:22–23 reads: "A stone that the builders threw out / has become the head of the corner. / From the LORD this came about; / in our eyes it is a marvel." In the psalm, Israel or its king, once despised, is now honored. There may be a Hebrew wordplay: ben (son) and 'even (stone), linking the son of 21:37 with the stone. The verse is quoted in Acts 4:11 and 1 Peter 2:7. "Head of the corner" may be the cornerstone of the foundation or the capstone at the top.

a: it will be given to a nation that yields its fruit
t: Taken from you, given to a nation
p: Only Matthew has this verse. Who is "you," and who is the "nation"? The answer has shaped Christian views of Israel.
b: Replacement reading: for much of church history this verse was read as God taking the kingdom from the Jewish people and giving it to the (largely Gentile) church as a "new Israel" (for example Justin Martyr and many later writers). Leaders reading: many scholars today note that the parable is spoken to the chief priests and Pharisees, who "understood that he meant them" (21:45); the kingdom is taken from them as Israel's stewards and given to a people, Jews and Gentiles, who bear fruit (Saldarini; Levine). Church as remnant: others see Matthew's community of Jewish and Gentile believers as the faithful Israel. Ethnos usually means "nation" or "people," and in the singular it does not mean "the Gentiles." See the chapter page and the "Where Christians differ" card.

a: Anyone who falls on this stone will be shattered
p: The stone that trips people (Isaiah 8:14–15) and the stone that crushes kingdoms (Daniel 2:34–35, 44–45).
b: Isaiah 8:14–15 calls the LORD "a stone to trip over" on which many will "fall and be broken." Daniel 2:34–35 and 2:44–45 tell of a stone, cut without hands, that strikes the statue of earthly kingdoms and turns it to chaff that the wind blows away. The verb likmaō means to winnow, to scatter like chaff, which matches Daniel's picture. Some manuscripts lack this verse (see the variant).

a: who took him for a prophet
p: The crowds kept the leaders from acting openly, so they would need a quiet arrest (26:4–5, 47).
b: At Passover Jerusalem was full of pilgrims, many of them from Galilee, and the authorities feared riots, which Roman troops would put down harshly. The leaders "feared the crowds" here and in 21:26 and 26:5. That is why the arrest will happen at night, away from the crowds, with a betrayer's help.

a: a king who put on a wedding for his son
p: The messianic banquet: Isaiah's feast for all peoples, and the wedding of God and his people.
b: Isaiah 25:6–9 pictures the LORD giving a feast for all peoples on Mount Zion. The prophets called God Israel's husband (Hosea 2:16–20; Isaiah 62:5), and Jesus called himself the bridegroom (9:15; 25:1–13). Luke tells a similar story of a man's great dinner, without a king, a son, armies or a wedding garment (Luke 14:16–24), and the Gospel of Thomas has another version (saying 64). Scholars debate whether these are one parable told differently or two.
r: Isaiah 25:6–9; 8:11; 9:15; 25:1–13; Luke 14:16–24; Revelation 19:7–9; Gospel of Thomas 64

a: summon the invited guests
p: Wealthy hosts sent a first invitation, then servants to call guests when the meal was ready.
b: Invitations went out in advance, then servants fetched the guests when everything was prepared (compare Esther 5:8; 6:14). Refusing at the second call after accepting the first was a grave insult to the host, still more to a king at his son's wedding.

a: set fire to their city
p: Many scholars hear the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 here. Others see a stock picture of a king's revenge.
b: The king's army burning the murderers' city is out of scale in a story about a wedding meal, and the verse is missing from Luke's version. Many critical scholars take it as Matthew's allusion to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, and use it to date the Gospel after that year. Others (for example Karl Rengstorf, Robert Gundry) argue that punishing a rebel city by fire was a common image in ancient literature and in the Old Testament (Judges 1:8; Isaiah 5:24–25), so it need not look back on AD 70, and could even be prophecy. Either way, Matthew's readers would have thought of the city's fall.

a: evil people and good people alike
p: The hall holds bad and good, like the field of wheat and weeds and the net with good and bad fish.
b: Matthew's church is a mixed company until the judgment (13:24–30, 47–50). The inclusion of the bad is grace; the inspection of the guests (22:11–13) is judgment. Augustine used the passage against the Donatists, who wanted a pure church of the righteous only (Sermon 90).

a: who had not put on clothes for a wedding
p: What does the garment stand for? Righteous deeds, love, faith, baptism, or Christ himself?
b: There is no clear ancient evidence that hosts handed out robes to guests, though many sermons assume it. In the Bible, clothing pictures a person's moral state (Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3:3–5; Revelation 19:8, where the bride's fine linen "stands for the right things God's people have done"). Readings: righteous living fitting the call (most modern scholars, in line with Matthew's stress on deeds, 5:20; 7:21); love (Augustine); baptism, the robe of the new life (some fathers); Christ's righteousness received by faith (many Reformation readers, Galatians 3:27). The man's silence shows he had no excuse.

a: There people will weep and grind their teeth
p: A banquet hall full of light, and outside the dark: Matthew's repeated picture of final exclusion.
b: Matthew uses "the darkness outside" three times (8:12; 22:13; 25:30) and "weeping and grinding of teeth" six times (also 13:42, 50; 24:51). Grinding teeth can show anger (Psalm 112:10; Acts 7:54) or anguish. The image is of being shut out of a lighted feast at night. How literally to take the pictures of judgment is discussed in the notes on 25:41–46.

a: For the called are many, but the chosen are few
p: "Called" means invited. "Chosen" are those who in the end are found fit. It is not a statement about predestination.
b: In Greek klētoi means "invited" (the same root as "call" in 22:3, 4, 8, 9) and eklektoi "chosen, picked out." The saying sums up the parable: many receive the invitation; few accept it rightly. Readers have used it in debates about election, some reading it as God's secret choice (Calvin), others as the free response of those invited (Wesley). Similar wording appears in 4 Ezra, a Jewish apocalypse of about AD 100, which says that many have been created but few will be saved (chapter 8).

a: the Herodians
p: Supporters of the Herod family, who backed Roman rule. Here they join the Pharisees.
b: The Herodians are named only here and in Mark (Mark 3:6; 12:13). They were probably supporters of Herod Antipas and his family, and so of Rome's system. The Pharisees were not friends of the Herods, so this pairing is striking: two groups who disagreed on the tax unite to trap Jesus. If he said "Pay," he would offend the many who hated Roman taxes; if he said "Do not pay," the Herodians could report him for rebellion.

a: the head tax to Caesar
p: A yearly tax on each person, paid to Rome since Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6.
b: When Rome made Judea a province in AD 6 and took a census for taxes, Judas the Galilean led a revolt, teaching that paying tribute to Rome meant accepting a human master instead of God (Josephus, War 2.118; Antiquities 18.4–10). The kēnsos (Latin census) was a head tax on adults. The question was a test of loyalty in a land where the issue had already cost lives.

a: Whose image is this
p: The silver denarius of Tiberius showed the emperor's head and called him son of the divine Augustus.
b: A denarius of Tiberius (emperor AD 14–37), the coin Rome's tribute was reckoned in, bore his portrait with the Latin inscription TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS, "Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, Augustus." To many devout Jews the image broke the command against images (Exodus 20:4), and the claim of divinity was worse. Jesus' opponents produce such a coin when asked, inside the temple courts. Jewish coins of the time avoided human images.

a: So pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God
p: The coin bears Caesar's image; people bear God's image. The saying has been read many ways.
b: "Give back" (apodote) means pay what is owed. The coin, stamped with Caesar's image, can go back to him. Many early readers (Tertullian, On Idolatry 15) noted that human beings bear God's image (Genesis 1:26–27), so a person owes God himself. Readings range from "two separate realms," church and state each with its own sphere (Luther), to "everything belongs to God, so Caesar's claim is limited" (many modern scholars), to "pay the tax, but do not worship the emperor." Paul gives practical advice in Romans 13:7. See the "Where Christians differ" card on the chapter page.

a: some Sadducees
p: A party of priestly aristocrats who accepted only what they found in the written Law, and denied the resurrection.
b: The Sadducees were linked to the high priestly families who ran the temple. Josephus says they rejected the Pharisees' traditions and held that souls perish with the body (Antiquities 18.16; War 2.164–166), and Acts 23:8 says they denied resurrection, angels and spirits. Their question uses the Law of Moses because that is the Scripture they accepted as binding. After the temple fell in AD 70 they disappear from history.

a: his brother must marry his widow and give his brother descendants
p: Deuteronomy 25:5–10 kept a dead man's name alive through a child born to his widow and his brother.
b: This site's Plain of Deuteronomy 25:5 reads: "Her husband's brother is to go in to her and take her as his wife, and do a brother-in-law's duty to her." The custom is called levirate marriage (Latin levir, brother-in-law); Ruth and Boaz show a wider form of it (Ruth 4). The Sadducees' story of seven husbands sounds like a deliberate echo of Tobit, where Sarah's seven husbands died one after another (Tobit 3:8). They mean to make resurrection look ridiculous.

a: They are like God's angels in heaven
p: Jesus does not say the raised become angels, but that they are like angels: deathless, so no need to marry.
b: Marriage in that world was largely about children and keeping a family line alive, the purpose of the levirate law. In the resurrection people no longer die (Luke 20:36, "they cannot die anymore"), so that purpose ends. 1 Enoch 15:6–7 says the same about angels: because they are immortal, God gave them no wives. Christians differ on what this means for married love after death; most hold that the bond of love is not lost though the institution ends, and Latter-day Saints teach that marriages sealed in the temple last forever. See the "Where Christians differ" card.

a: God is not God of dead people but of living ones
p: God named himself the God of the patriarchs long after they died. So they must live to him.
b: Jesus quotes God's words to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:6). Because God bound himself in covenant to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, his faithfulness cannot end at their death. Later rabbis also looked for the resurrection in the Torah: the Talmud finds it in Exodus 6:4, where God promises to give the land "to them," the patriarchs themselves (Sanhedrin 90b). 4 Maccabees says the martyrs, "like Abraham, Isaac and Jacob," live to God (4 Maccabees 7:19; 16:25).

a: a lawyer
p: Not a courtroom lawyer: a scholar of the law of Moses, here a Pharisee.
b: Nomikos means an expert in the nomos, the Law. Matthew uses the word only here (some manuscripts lack it; see the variant). In Mark the questioner is a friendly scribe whom Jesus praises (Mark 12:28–34); in Matthew he comes "as a test," part of the series of challenges in 22:15–46. In Luke a lawyer asks a different question that leads to the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37).

a: which commandment in the law is the great one?
p: Rabbis counted 613 commands and debated which were "heavy" and which "light."
b: Later rabbis counted 613 commandments in the Torah (Talmud, Makkot 23b) and spoke of "light" and "heavy" ones (Mishnah Avot 2:1). Some tried to sum up the whole Law: Hillel told a would-be convert, "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor; that is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary" (Talmud, Shabbat 31a). Rabbi Akiva called Leviticus 19:18 "a great principle of the Torah" (Sifra on Leviticus 19:18). So the question was a known one; the test was whether Jesus would rank any command above others or set any aside.

a: with all your heart, with all your being and with all your mind
p: Deuteronomy 6:5, part of the prayer every devout Jew said morning and evening.
b: This site's Plain of Deuteronomy 6:5 reads: "Love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength." Matthew's quotation has "heart, being (psychē, soul or life), and mind" (dianoia), not "strength"; Mark and Luke have four terms including both mind and strength. Some Greek copies of Deuteronomy have "mind" for heart. The Shema ("Hear, O Israel") was recited daily (Mishnah Berakhot 1:1–2). Note that the Plain follows Deuteronomy 6:5's site wording, "being," for psychē.

a: A second one is like it
p: Joining love of God and love of neighbor was not new to Jesus, but making them the hinge of all Scripture was striking.
b: The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, a Jewish work in Christian hands, already pairs them: "Love the Lord and your neighbor" (Testament of Issachar 5:2; Testament of Dan 5:3). Philo calls piety toward God and justice toward people the two chief headings of the Law (Special Laws 2.63). "Like it" means of equal weight. Jesus in Matthew also sums up the Law with the Golden Rule (7:12). Love here is a matter of action and loyalty, not only feeling (Leviticus 19:9–18 lists concrete acts).

a: The whole law hangs from these two commandments
p: Like a door on its hinges or a weight on a peg: the rest of Scripture depends on these two.
b: The verb krematai, "hangs," matches a rabbinic expression for a teaching that "hangs on" a verse, depends on it. "The Law and the Prophets" means the Scriptures as a whole (5:17; 7:12). Jesus does not say the other commandments are cancelled, but that they are to be read through these two (compare 23:23).

a: Whose son is he?
p: Jewish hope expected a king from David's line. Jesus asks how David can call his own descendant "Lord."
b: God promised David a son whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16), and the prophets looked for a shoot from Jesse's stump (Isaiah 11:1). The Psalms of Solomon, written in Jerusalem in the first century BC, pray for "the son of David" to rule Israel (17:21). Jesus does not deny that the Messiah is David's son; Matthew opened by calling Jesus "son of David" (1:1). His riddle says the Messiah is more than David's son.

a: The Lord said to my Lord
p: The Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most often. Jesus assumes David wrote it about the Messiah.
b: This site's Plain of Psalm 110:1 reads: "The LORD declares to my lord: / 'Sit at my right hand, / until I set your enemies down / as a stool for your feet.'" In Hebrew the first "Lord" is YHWH and the second adoni, "my lord"; in Greek both are kyrios. The psalm's title names David, and Jesus and his hearers took it as David's words about the Messiah. Many modern scholars think it was written for a king of David's line, perhaps by a court poet. Later rabbinic tradition applied it to Abraham (Talmud, Nedarim 32b) or to the Messiah. The New Testament uses it for Jesus' exaltation (26:64; Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13).

a: Then Jesus addressed the crowds and his disciples
p: The woes are spoken to the crowds and disciples about the scribes and Pharisees, then turned on them directly.
b: Chapter 23 begins as a warning to Jesus' followers and the crowds (23:1–12), then addresses the scribes and Pharisees in the second person (23:13–36), and ends with a lament over Jerusalem (23:37–39). Many scholars hear in its sharpness the conflict between Matthew's community and the synagogue leaders of his own day, after AD 70, when the Pharisees' heirs were shaping Judaism. Reading it with that history in mind does not soften the words, but it keeps readers from taking it as a portrait of all Jews or of Judaism. See the chapter page.

a: On Moses' seat
p: Probably the place of the teacher who explained the Law, possibly a real stone chair in synagogues.
b: "Moses' seat" means the authority to teach the Law Moses gave. Stone chairs have been found in ancient synagogues at Chorazin, Hammath Tiberias and Delos, and some scholars call them "seats of Moses," though they date mostly from after Jesus' time. A later midrash speaks of the "chair" (qatedra) of Moses (Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 1:7). The verb is past tense, "have sat down": some read it neutrally (they hold the office), others as a hint that they took the seat for themselves.

a: So whatever they say to you, do it and keep it
p: A puzzle: Jesus elsewhere rejects the Pharisees' traditions (15:1–20; 16:12). How can he say "do whatever they say"?
b: Readings: (1) Jesus means their reading of Moses' Law itself, not their added traditions (Chrysostom). (2) It is irony: do what they say, if you can; the rest of the chapter shows it is not worth doing. (3) It keeps an early layer from a Jewish-Christian group that still followed Pharisaic teaching, as Matthew's own community may once have done. (4) The point is the contrast: their words are better than their lives. (5) Mark Allan Powell argues that "Moses' seat" names their role as keepers and readers of the Torah scrolls, so "whatever they say" means what they read aloud from Moses. Many Jewish readers note that the charge "they say and do not do" was also made by the rabbis themselves against unworthy teachers (Mishnah Avot 1:17; Talmud, Sotah 22b, on seven kinds of Pharisees).

a: They bundle up heavy burdens
p: Their strict rules weigh on others, while Jesus says his own yoke is light (11:28–30).
b: The image is a load of rules tied like bundles on a porter's back. Jesus contrasts it with "My yoke is kind to wear, and the load I give is light" (11:30). Jewish teachers spoke of "the yoke of the commandments" positively, as a joy (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2), and many Jewish scholars point out that the Pharisees often made the Law easier to live, not harder, for example in their rules for the Sabbath. Jesus' charge here is that they "will not budge" the burdens: that is, they do nothing to help people carry them, or they find ways for themselves around them.

a: phylacteries
p: Small leather boxes holding Scripture passages, tied on the forehead and arm during prayer.
b: Jews still wear tefillin, which take literally the command to bind God's words "on your hand" and "between your eyes" (Deuteronomy 6:8; 11:18; Exodus 13:9, 16). Some from the first century were found at Qumran, holding tiny scrolls with the Ten Commandments and the Shema. The Greek name phylaktērion, "safeguard," also meant an amulet, but Jews did not use them as charms. Jesus' complaint is not about wearing them but about making them larger for show.

a: make their tassels bigger
p: The tassels on the corners of clothes, commanded in Numbers 15:38. Jesus wore them too.
b: The Law told Israelites to put tassels (tsitsit) with a blue cord on the corners of their clothes to remember the commandments (Numbers 15:37–41; Deuteronomy 22:12). The woman who was healed touched the tassel of Jesus' cloak (9:20; 14:36). So the issue is again length for display, not the custom itself.

a: having people call them 'Rabbi.'
p: "My great one," a title of respect for a teacher. Only after AD 70 did it become a formal title for ordained sages.
b: Rabbi is Hebrew for "my master, my great one." In Jesus' time it was a respectful way to address any teacher (John 1:38 explains it as "Teacher"). After the temple fell, it became the title of the ordained sages who shaped rabbinic Judaism. Matthew's use may reflect his own day, when "rabbi" was becoming the title of the synagogue's leaders. In Matthew only Judas calls Jesus "Rabbi" (26:25, 49).

a: Do not call anyone on earth your 'father,' either
p: A warning against status and rank among disciples. Churches differ on whether it rules out titles like "Father."
b: Jewish teachers were sometimes called "father" (abba), as in "Abba Saul" in the Mishnah, and founders of schools were "fathers." Jesus' point is that his followers form one family under one Father and one Teacher (23:8–10; 12:50). Yet Paul calls himself the Corinthians' father in the gospel (1 Corinthians 4:15), and Stephen addresses elders as "fathers" (Acts 7:2). Catholic, Orthodox and many Anglican Christians call priests "Father" and read the verse as a warning against putting any human in God's place; Quakers and others have avoided such titles. See the "Where Christians differ" card.

a: Anyone who raises himself up will be brought low
p: A saying Jesus repeats in several settings, rooted in the Hebrew Bible's songs of reversal.
b: The same saying appears in Luke 14:11 and 18:14. It echoes Proverbs 29:23, Ezekiel 21:26, and the songs of Hannah and Mary, where God brings down the proud and lifts the lowly (1 Samuel 2:7–8; Luke 1:52). The passive voice ("will be brought low") points to God as the one who acts.

a: woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!
p: "Woe" is a prophet's cry of grief and warning. It is not a curse.
b: Ouai, "woe," is the cry of mourning at a funeral (1 Kings 13:30) that prophets used to announce coming disaster (Isaiah 5:8–23 has six woes; Amos 5:18; 6:1; Habakkuk 2:6–19). It mixes anger and sorrow, which is why the chapter ends in lament (23:37). Matthew has seven woes (23:13, 15, 16, 23, 25, 27, 29). "Hypocrite" was the word for a stage actor: someone playing a part (see 6:2).

a: You lock up the kingdom of heaven right in front of people
p: The teachers who held the "keys" of knowledge are accused of keeping people out.
b: Luke's version says "You have carried off the key to knowledge" (Luke 11:52). The image of keys recalls Peter's "keys of the kingdom" (16:19). As teachers, the scribes and Pharisees held the means to open the Scriptures to others. Jesus accuses them of opposing his message and so turning people away from the kingdom he announced.

a: to make one convert
p: Did Jews seek converts? The "convert" may be a Gentile, or a Jew won over to the Pharisees' way.
b: Some Jews actively won Gentile converts (proselytes) in this era: Josephus tells how the royal house of Adiabene became Jewish, and how a Galilean named Eleazar, known for his strictness about the Law, urged King Izates to be circumcised (Antiquities 20.34–48). Other scholars, such as Scot McKnight and Martin Goodman, argue that Jews did not run organized missions, and that Jesus means winning a fellow Jew to the Pharisees' strict way. "A son of Gehenna" means someone headed for and belonging to judgment; on Gehenna see 5:22.

a: If someone takes an oath by the sanctuary, that counts for nothing
p: Jewish law debated which oath formulas were binding. Jesus mocks any system that lets people escape a promise.
b: The Mishnah discusses vows made "by" the temple, the altar or the offerings, and which forms bind (Mishnah Nedarim 1:3), and says an oath "by heaven and by earth" does not bind (Mishnah Shevuot 4:13). The rabbis' aim was often to protect people from rash words. Jesus' complaint is that a scale of more and less binding oaths makes room for dishonesty. He has already said not to swear at all but to let a yes be yes (5:33–37). The "sanctuary" (naos) is the temple building itself, as distinct from the whole temple area (hieron, 21:12).

a: Foolish and blind!
p: Jesus warned against calling a brother "fool" (5:22). Here he uses the word himself.
b: In 5:22 Jesus warns that whoever says "You fool!" (mōre) will face the fire of Gehenna. Here he calls the Pharisees mōroi. Interpreters explain the tension in different ways: 5:22 forbids contempt and anger toward a brother, while here Jesus speaks as a prophet passing God's judgment on false teaching (as Psalm 14:1 calls the godless a fool); or the words of 5:22 are about insults spoken in rage. Some readers simply note the tension honestly.

a: You pay a tithe on mint and dill and cumin
p: The Law required a tenth of the harvest. Pharisees took this carefully even for garden herbs.
b: The Law required a tenth of grain, wine, oil and produce (Leviticus 27:30; Deuteronomy 14:22–23). Pharisees extended it to everything eaten that grows from the ground, and the Mishnah discusses tithing dill's seeds, leaves and stalks (Mishnah Ma'aserot 4:5). Jesus does not reject the practice: "These you should have done, and not let go of the others." His charge is lost proportion.

a: justice, mercy and faithfulness
p: An echo of Micah 6:8 and Hosea 6:6: justice, loyal love and walking faithfully with God.
b: Micah 6:8 asks what the LORD requires: to do justice, to love loyal love (hesed), and to walk humbly with your God. Jesus has twice quoted Hosea 6:6, "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" (9:13; 12:7). Pistis usually means faith, but here, next to justice and mercy, it means faithfulness, being trustworthy. "Heavier" matches the rabbinic language of "heavy" and "light" commandments (see 22:36).
orig: τὴν κρίσιν καὶ τὸ ἔλεος καὶ τὴν πίστιν

a: filtering out the gnat and gulping down the camel
p: Both were unclean animals. In Aramaic the words may have sounded alike: galma and gamla.
b: Careful Jews strained wine through cloth to avoid swallowing a tiny insect, which the Law counts as unclean (Leviticus 11:20–23, 41–43). The camel was also unclean (Leviticus 11:4), and the largest animal in the land (see 19:24). Many scholars suggest a play on Aramaic qalma or galma (gnat, louse) and gamla (camel). It is a joke that bites: careful about the smallest rule, careless about the biggest.

a: You wash the outside of the cup and the plate
p: Jewish purity law treated a vessel's outside and inside separately. Jesus turns it into a picture of the heart.
b: The Mishnah distinguishes the outer and inner surfaces of a vessel: one may be impure while the other is pure (Mishnah Kelim 25:1). Jacob Neusner argued that Jesus' saying touches a real debate between the schools of Shammai and Hillel about which part of a cup counts. Jesus moves the question from vessels to people: what fills the cup is gained by grabbing and greed. Luke's version says "your own inside is filled with what you have grabbed and with wickedness" (Luke 11:39).

a: tombs painted with whitewash
p: Graves were marked with white lime so pilgrims would not touch them and become unclean.
b: Touching a corpse or a grave made a person ritually unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), which would keep a pilgrim from the Passover. So before the festivals, graves were marked with lime (Mishnah Shekalim 1:1; Ma'aser Sheni 5:1). A whitewashed tomb looked bright and clean, yet it warned of uncleanness inside. Jesus' picture is sharp: the Pharisees, who worked hard to avoid impurity, are like the very source of impurity.

a: You put up tombs for the prophets
p: In Jesus' day monuments to holy figures were being built around Jerusalem.
b: Herod the Great built a white marble monument at the entrance of David's tomb (Josephus, Antiquities 16.179–183). Large tomb monuments from this era still stand in the Kidron Valley, one later called the Tomb of Zechariah. Honoring the prophets was a pious act. Jesus' charge is that honoring dead prophets while rejecting living ones proves the family likeness: "sons" act like their "fathers" (23:31–32).

a: fill up your fathers' measure!
p: An image of sin piling up until judgment comes, as with the Amorites in Genesis 15:16.
b: God told Abraham his descendants would not receive the land yet, because "the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full" (Genesis 15:16). The idea is that judgment waits until a people's sin is full. Paul uses the same image of those who opposed the gospel in Judea (1 Thessalonians 2:16). Jesus' command is bitter irony, not real encouragement.

a: Offspring of vipers!
p: John the Baptist's words (3:7), used by Jesus in 12:34 and here.
b: The phrase pictures snakes fleeing a burning field, or a brood that shares its parents' poison. John used it of Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism (3:7), and Jesus of Pharisees in 12:34. The repetition ties John's warning and Jesus' warning together, as in 21:25–32.

a: prophets, wise men and scribes
p: Jesus sends his own messengers, using the titles of Jewish teachers. Matthew's church had its own prophets and scribes.
b: In Luke the sender is "the Wisdom of God" (Luke 11:49); in Matthew Jesus speaks as the sender. The titles are Jewish ones, and Matthew's community seems to have had Christian prophets and scribes (10:41; 13:52). Flogging in synagogues was a real synagogue punishment (Deuteronomy 25:2–3; 2 Corinthians 11:24), and crucifixion was Roman. The verse reflects Christian experience of persecution in the decades after Jesus (10:17–23; Acts 7:58; 12:2).

a: from the blood of Abel the righteous to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah
p: Abel is the Bible's first murder victim, Zechariah the last in Hebrew order. His father's name is a puzzle.
b: Abel's blood cried from the ground (Genesis 4:10). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned "in the court of the LORD's house" and said as he died, "May the LORD see it, and may he seek it out" (2 Chronicles 24:22). Since Chronicles comes last in the Hebrew Bible, "from Abel to Zechariah" means all the martyrs from first to last. But Matthew calls him "son of Berechiah," the name of the father of the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1). Explanations: Matthew confused the two; a copyist added the name (Codex Sinaiticus as first written lacks "son of Berechiah"; see the variant); the name refers to Zechariah son of Baris, killed in the temple by Zealots in AD 67–68 (Josephus, War 4.334–344); or Jehoiada was a grandfather. Luke 11:51 has no father's name. Jerome reports a gospel used by Jewish Christians that read "son of Jehoiada."
r: Genesis 4:8–10; 2 Chronicles 24:20–22; Zechariah 1:1; Luke 11:50–51; Hebrews 11:4; Hebrews 12:24

a: it will all fall on this generation
p: Many link the judgment to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, within the lifetime of Jesus' hearers.
b: "This generation" in Matthew means Jesus' contemporaries (11:16; 12:39–45; 24:34). The judgment is the destruction of the temple and city, which the next verses and chapter 24 describe. The verse has been misused to blame Jewish people of every age for Jesus' death; the text speaks of one generation and one event, and most churches today reject the charge of collective guilt (Nostra Aetate 4). See the chapter page.

a: the way a bird gathers her young under her wings
p: A mother bird's wings: an image the Bible uses for God's protecting care.
b: Scripture speaks of shelter under God's wings (Deuteronomy 32:11; Psalm 17:8; 36:7; 91:4; Ruth 2:12). Later Jewish writers spoke of converts coming "under the wings of the Shekhinah," God's presence. Jesus uses a homely picture, a hen with her chicks, for his own longing to gather Jerusalem's people. "How many times" suggests more visits to Jerusalem than Matthew tells, as John's Gospel reports.
r: Deuteronomy 32:11; Psalm 17:8; Psalm 91:4; Ruth 2:12; Isaiah 31:5; Luke 13:34–35

a: your house is abandoned to you
p: The temple, God's house, will be left without God and then destroyed (24:1–2).
b: "Your house" is the temple, or Jerusalem itself. Jeremiah warned: "I have left my house" (Jeremiah 12:7) and "this house will become a ruin" (Jeremiah 22:5). Ezekiel saw God's glory leave the temple before the Babylonians destroyed it (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). Immediately after these words Jesus leaves the temple and predicts its destruction (24:1–2).

a: until you say, 'Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name!'
p: Does Jerusalem's welcome come too late, or is this a promise that Israel will one day greet its Messiah?
b: Some read the verse as judgment: when they see him again, at his coming in glory, they will have to acknowledge him, but too late. Others read it as hope: "until" sets a condition, and Jerusalem will one day bless the one who comes, as Paul hopes that "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26). Dale Allison argued that it is a conditional prophecy: the time of his coming depends on Israel's welcome. The words are Psalm 118:26, which the crowds already sang at his entry (21:9).
